---
title: "Serfling"
---

## Overview {#sec-serfl-overview}

Every method so far has asked whether this week is unusual for this time of year.
The Farrington chapter ended on a question that kind of method cannot answer — has
the epidemic season started? — because a normal seasonal rise is, by construction,
not unusual for its time of year. Serfling's method models what the year would look
like with no epidemic in it, and treats anything well above that line as epidemic
activity. Like a tide table, which predicts the water level from a few regular
cycles so that a storm surge is whatever it did not predict, Serfling's baseline is a
slow trend plus a few waves of fixed length, fitted to years with the epidemics taken
out.

Robert E. Serfling published the method in 1963 at the US Communicable Disease
Center (CDC), to monitor weekly deaths from pneumonia and influenza (P&I) in 108 US
cities [@serfling1963]. He chose P&I deaths although they lag influenza cases by
about four weeks, because case reports and school or work absences were not
quantitative enough or not available widely. A **parametric periodic regression**
model, it remains sixty years on one of the foundations of epidemic thresholds
[@unkel2012].

For a seasonal disease one fixed threshold does not work: low enough to catch an
epidemic outside the season, it fires all through the peak season; high enough for
the peak season, it misses epidemics outside it. Serfling lets the threshold move
with the seasonal baseline.

::: {.callout-note title="Core idea"}
Epidemic threshold = the expected level with no epidemic + a safety margin for
random variation. The variants of Serfling differ mainly in how they estimate these
two components.
:::

## The procedure at a glance {#sec-serfl-glance}

The method rests on three ideas: a baseline built from a long-term trend and sine
and cosine waves (a Fourier series); training data cleaned of past epidemics, so
that they do not pull the baseline up; and a threshold a margin above the baseline,
usually 1.64–1.645 standard deviations of the error, that must be crossed two weeks
in a row [@serfling1963]. In practice that is four steps (@fig-serfl-glance).
@sec-serfl-math builds the model behind step 2; @sec-serfl-steps details each step
and works through all four on one data set.

::: {#fig-serfl-glance}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serfl-glance"></div>
```

Serfling's procedure on simulated weekly data. Click a step to read it in full.
:::

## Mathematical basis {#sec-serfl-math}

### The general equation {#sec-serfl-equation}

The Serfling model with $r$ harmonics has the form [@serfling1963]:

$$
E\left(Y_t\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{i=1}^{r}\left[\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-serfl-general}

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $Y_t$ | Observed value of the surveillance indicator at time $t$ (cases, deaths, a percentage...) |
| $t$ | Continuous time index, $t = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ |
| $\beta_0$ | Intercept: the mean baseline level at the time origin |
| $\beta_1$ | Long-term (secular) trend coefficient, reflecting changes in population or in the reporting system |
| $L$ | Length of one annual cycle: 52 for weekly data, 13 for four-week periods (as in the original paper), 12 for monthly data |
| $r$ | Number of harmonics included in the model |
| $\gamma_i,\ \delta_i$ | Coefficients of the cosine and sine waves of harmonic $i$ |

: Symbols in the Serfling equation. {#tbl-serfl-symbols}

Each parameter has one job (@fig-serfl-equation): $\beta_0$ sets the level,
$\beta_1$ tilts the curve from year to year, and each pair $\gamma_i,\ \delta_i$ sets
how tall one seasonal wave is and when it peaks. The trend can also be quadratic or
cubic when the data change nonlinearly [@pelat2007]. Serfling wrote the equation as
$\hat{Y} = u + bt + \sum a_i\cos\theta + \sum b_i\sin\theta$, with $\theta$ linear in
$t$ [@serfling1963]; this lesson uses $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ to avoid clashing
with later notation.

::: {#fig-serfl-equation}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serfl-equation"></div>
```

@eq-serfl-general over three years of weekly data ($L = 52$): the dotted line is the
trend, the blue curve adds the seasonal waves. The starting values are the true
baseline of the data in @sec-serfl-walk.
:::

### Fourier series, intuitively {#sec-serfl-fourier}

Any curve that repeats every year can be assembled from sine and cosine waves of
different frequencies, as a chord is built from single notes. **Harmonic 1** has
period $L$ (52 weeks) and rises and falls once a year; **harmonic 2** has period
$L/2$ (26 weeks) and rises and falls twice; **harmonic** $i$ rises and falls $i$
times. At each harmonic, the cosine–sine pair is one wave with an amplitude and a
phase:

$$
\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) = A_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L} - \theta_i\right),\qquad A_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i^2 + \delta_i^2}
$$

$A_i$ is how tall the wave is and $\theta_i$ when it peaks. The cosine alone peaks at
the start of the cycle, the sine alone a quarter of a cycle later; mixing them in
the ratio $\gamma_i : \delta_i$ puts the peak in any week. And because $\gamma_i$ and
$\delta_i$ enter the model linearly, ordinary linear regression estimates them; no
nonlinear fit of the phase is needed. The analyst chooses only $L$ and $r$: the
frequencies are fixed, and the data decide how tall each wave is and where it peaks.

@fig-serfl-fit lets you do the regression's job by hand: set the four coefficients
until your curve runs through a year of weekly data, then compare with least
squares, which makes the squared distances as small as possible.

::: {#fig-serfl-fit}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serfl-fit"></div>
```

Fitting a Fourier series by hand. Amber lines are the distances from each week to
your curve. A symmetric peak needs only harmonic 1; a lopsided peak, or two peaks a
year, also needs harmonic 2.
:::

**The first-order model** ($r = 1$) gives exactly one symmetric peak a year:

$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \varepsilon_t
$$

**The second-order model** ($r = 2$) adds a semi-annual wave, allowing two peaks a
year or one asymmetric peak that rises fast and falls slowly:

$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \gamma_2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \delta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \varepsilon_t
$$

A larger $r$ follows more complex shapes, but pushed too far the model fits random
noise and leftover epidemic peaks as well. So $r$ is chosen by a statistical test,
not by eye.

### Choosing the number of harmonics: the example in the original paper {#sec-serfl-1963}

Serfling fitted the model to P&I deaths in 108 US cities over three seasons without
a major epidemic (leaving out the 1957–58 pandemic), in thirteen four-week periods a
year [@serfling1963]. To decide on a second harmonic he used Bliss's analysis of
variance, a partial F test: the variance added by harmonic 2 (mean square 8,136) was
smaller than the residual variance of the second-order model (13,157), so
$F \approx 0.62 < 1$. Harmonic 2 explained no more than noise, and the first-order
model was kept:

$$
\hat{Y}_t = 300.5 + 2.1\, t + 97.6\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{13} - 2.67\right)
$$ {#eq-serfl-1963}

Here $t$ is in four-week periods, from the midpoint of the period ending 24 September
1955. In this amplitude–phase form the amplitude is 97.6 deaths per week and the peak
falls at $t = 2.67 \times 13/2\pi \approx 5.5$, around February 1956
(@fig-serfl-1963). In R the same test is `anova(m1, m2)`; models can also be compared
by AIC [@pelat2007].

::: {#fig-serfl-1963}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-1963"></div>
```

Reconstructed from Serfling (1963). (a) The baseline from @eq-serfl-1963 and an
illustrative epidemic threshold, set 1.64 times the weekly standard deviation (27.9
deaths) reported by Serfling above the baseline; in the original paper the standard
deviation was also corrected for the extrapolated trend, so this gap widens over
time. (b) The analysis of variance used to choose the number of harmonics. Hover
panel (a) to read any period.
:::

## Computing an epidemic threshold with Serfling {#sec-serfl-steps}

The four steps of @fig-serfl-glance, in detail. Throughout, the aim is to separate
ordinary baseline variation from what past epidemics left behind.

::: {#serfl-step-1 .algo-step}
**1. Clean the history.** Remove or downweight past epidemics before fitting, so the
baseline describes a year without them. Five ways are in use:

- **By calendar.** Drop seasons or weeks known to be epidemic. Serfling used only
  non-epidemic seasons, replaced isolated high weeks with the trend value when
  estimating the spread, and, when many years in a row had epidemics, estimated the
  trend from the low season alone, roughly mid-May to mid-September [@serfling1963].
  EuroMOMO fits only spring and autumn weeks, least affected by winter influenza and
  summer heat [@euromomo].
- **By percentile.** Drop a fixed share of the highest training weeks, typically
  about 15% [@pelat2007; @pelat2017]; on French influenza-like illness data the best
  configuration cut at the 86th percentile and used the full history [@souty2018].
- **Iteratively.** Fit, drop the weeks above the fitted line and refit; then drop
  weeks above the upper 95% prediction limit and refit, until $R^2$ stops increasing
  [@wang2015].
- **Robustly.** Keep every week but fit by iteratively reweighted estimation, such as
  `MASS::rlm`, so unusual weeks lose weight on their own [@pelat2017]. The CDC's P&I
  baseline used a robust procedure [@cdc1998].
- **As censored.** Treat each epidemic week as left-censored — without the epidemic
  it would have been at most what was observed — and mark weeks as epidemic one at a
  time, largest positive residual first, up to a set share (about 16% for acute
  respiratory infection) [@prochazka2016].
:::

::: {#serfl-step-2 .algo-step}
**2. Fit and extrapolate.** Estimate the coefficients on the cleaned data (by least
squares, or a weighted or likelihood variant) and project $\hat Y_t$ over the weeks to
be monitored. That projection is the **seasonal baseline**, what to expect with no
epidemic. Five years of training is common [@euromomo; @pelat2017] but worth
testing: on the French data the full history beat windows of 3, 5 or 10 years
[@souty2018].
:::

::: {#serfl-step-3 .algo-step}
**3. Set the threshold.** Even with no epidemic the series scatters around the
baseline, so the threshold sits a multiple of the forecast error above it:

$$ \text{Threshold}_t = \hat Y_t + z_\alpha\,\hat\sigma_t, $$

where $\hat\sigma_t$, the standard deviation of the forecast error, combines the
residual spread with the uncertainty of extrapolating. Serfling and the CDC use
$z = 1.64$–$1.645$ [@serfling1963; @cdc1998]; Serfling corrected for the extrapolated
trend but not for the Fourier terms. This is the upper end of a one-sided 95% (or
two-sided 90%) prediction interval, `level = 0.90` in R's `predict()`
[@mcconeghy_flumodelr]. Santé publique France uses $z \approx 1.96$, trading
sensitivity for specificity [@pelat2017]. On a log-normal model the threshold is
$\exp(\hat\mu_t + z_\alpha\hat\sigma)$, computed on the log scale [@prochazka2016].
:::

::: {#serfl-step-4 .algo-step}
**4. Require two weeks.** A single high week is as often a reporting delay or a data
error as an epidemic. The onset is declared only when the series stays above the
threshold **two weeks in a row** [@serfling1963; @wang2015].
:::

### Working through the four steps {#sec-serfl-walk}

Step 1 decides the quality of the whole method: fit raw history and every past
epidemic pulls the baseline up and swells the residual spread, so the threshold lands
too high and new epidemics are flagged late [@unkel2012]. @fig-serfl-walk simulates
five training seasons, each with a winter epidemic, and a sixth to monitor. Because
the data are simulated, the true baseline is known, and so is the real false alarm
rate of any threshold. Choose a cleaning method, step through, then switch methods at
any step to compare.

::: {#fig-serfl-walk}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serfl-walk"></div>
```

The four steps on simulated weekly data (season week 1 is July; noise standard
deviation 10). Amber rings mark training weeks dropped or downweighted; the grey line
is the true baseline, which the method never sees. All methods use $z = 1.645$.
:::

| Cleaning | Weeks used | Residual $s$ | Baseline minus truth, this season | Real weekly false alarm rate | Alarm before the peak |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| None | 260 | 21.9 | −9.3 to +30.6 | 0.05% | 1 week |
| Calendar, weeks 14–40 | 125 | 9.5 | −2.1 to −0.2 | 6.0% | 4 weeks |
| Percentile, 15% | 221 | 10.5 | −1.4 to +7.7 | 2.4% | 2 weeks |
| Percentile, 25% | 197 | 9.4 | −0.4 to +0.4 | 5.8% | 4 weeks |
| Iterative | 140 | 8.6 | −10.5 to +10.5 | 11.9% | 2 weeks |
| Robust (Huber) | 260, weighted | 14.4 | −6.1 to +21.5 | 0.8% | 1 week |

: The cleaning methods in @fig-serfl-walk, against a nominal false alarm rate of 5%.
{#tbl-serfl-trim}

Untrimmed, the threshold barely fires and the epidemic is confirmed one week before
its peak. Each cleaning method succeeds or fails for its own reason:

- **Calendar** does best here because every epidemic falls inside the window (weeks
  14–40, roughly October to March); it fails when one does not, and it leaves fewer
  weeks to fit.
- **Percentile** is only as good as its share, which should be roughly the share of
  weeks actually epidemic: a quarter here, while the common 15% was tuned on French
  influenza-like illness [@souty2018]. Trim 40% and the normal seasonal peak goes too;
  an ordinary week then crosses the threshold almost one time in five.
- **Iterative** cleaning drops every week above the first fitted line, here 75
  ordinary weeks with 45 epidemic ones, so the baseline ends about 10 too low in
  summer and 10 too high in winter, and $s$ underestimates the noise.
- **Robust** regression only reduces the weight of large residuals; with a quarter of
  the weeks epidemic, they still pull the baseline up. On the French data, too, it was
  less sensitive than periodic regression with trimming [@souty2018].

Cleaning also decides $r$: untrimmed, the test for a second harmonic gives
$F = 27.8$, because the extra wave chases the epidemic peaks; at 15% trimming it falls
to 1.6 (step 2 of the figure).

### Why two weeks in a row {#sec-serfl-twoweek}

With $z = 1.645$ an ordinary week still crosses the threshold about 5% of the time,
two to three weeks a year [@serfling1963]. Over a 26-week winter–spring with no
epidemic and independent weeks, the chance that at least one crosses is
$1 - 0.95^{26} = 0.736$. Two weeks in a row leaves 25 adjacent pairs, each crossing
with probability $0.05^2$, so the chance falls to at most $25 \times 0.0025 = 0.0625$
— exactly 0.058; Serfling quoted about one in ten.

The price is time. The chance that a genuine rise is still unflagged after its second
week is 0.9 for a moderate epidemic and 0.7 for a large one; after the third, 0.1 and
under 0.01 [@serfling1963]. The arithmetic also assumes independent weeks; Serfling
noted they are slightly correlated, and at a correlation of 0.4 the two-week false
alarm rate triples, to about 17.5% (@fig-serfl-twoweek).

::: {#fig-serfl-twoweek}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-twoweek"></div>
```

Serfling's argument, simulated. Each bar is one week of a 26-week season, in
standard deviations from the baseline. Amber weeks cross the line alone; red weeks
are confirmed by the week before. Simulate many seasons, then raise $\rho$.
:::

### Excess burden {#sec-serfl-excess}

Once the epidemic period is identified, the model also estimates the excess burden,
in one of two ways:

- **Against the baseline:** $\text{Excess}_t = Y_t - \hat{Y}_t$, summed over the
  epidemic weeks [@serfling1963].
- **Against the threshold (more conservative):**
  $\text{Excess}_t = \max\left(Y_t - \text{Threshold}_t,\ 0\right)$, counting only the
  part above the threshold [@mcconeghy_flumodelr].

## Variants and practical implementation {#sec-serfl-variants}

### P&I mortality surveillance at the US CDC {#sec-serfl-cdc}

The CDC applied Serfling to the **percentage of all deaths due to pneumonia and
influenza**; a percentage is less biased than a count when the number of reporting
units changes from week to week. The baseline came from periodic regression with a
robust procedure, and the threshold was 1.645 standard deviations above it
[@cdc1998]. In October 2016 the data source moved from the 122 Cities Mortality
Reporting System to the mortality surveillance system of the National Center for
Health Statistics (NCHS) [@cdc2016].

### Serfling–Poisson and EuroMOMO {#sec-serfl-euromomo}

Least squares assumes normal residuals with constant variance: reasonable for large
counts, poor for small or sparse ones, or counts split by age group and small area
[@unkel2012]. The remedy is a generalised linear model (GLM) with a log link and a
Poisson distribution corrected for overdispersion (quasi-Poisson):

$$
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \log\left(N_t\right) + \eta_0 + \eta_1 t + \eta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \eta_3\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right)
$$

where $\mu_t$ is the expected count and $\log\left(N_t\right)$ a population offset,
included when population data exist so that the model estimates a rate.

This is the structure of **EuroMOMO** (European monitoring of excess mortality): a
quasi-Poisson GLM with a linear trend and an annual sine wave, fitted on the spring
and autumn weeks of up to five previous years, with a correction for delays in death
registration [@euromomo]. **FluMOMO** adds influenza activity and extreme
temperatures as explanatory variables [@nielsen2018]; **the modulation model** lets
the trend and the seasonal amplitude change smoothly over time through P-splines
[@leger2025].

### Implementation in R {#sec-serfl-r}

| Variant | Package / function | Main syntax | Handling past epidemics and the threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serfling OLS | `stats::lm`, `predict` | `lm(y ~ t + sin(2*pi*t/52) + cos(2*pi*t/52), data = df_clean)` | Trim before fitting. The threshold is the upper limit of `predict(..., interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)` [@mcconeghy_flumodelr] |
| Automatic Serfling | `flumodelr::fluserf` | `fluserf(data = df, outc = perc_fludeaths, time = yrweek_dt)` | By default fits only on June–September (treating October–May as the influenza season). Returns the baseline `y0` and the threshold `y0_ul` [@mcconeghy_flumodelr] |
| Robust Serfling | `MASS::rlm` | Same formula, fitted on a sliding 261-week window (from $w - 261$ to $w - 1$) | No trimming beforehand; the algorithm downweights unusually high weeks automatically [@pelat2017] |
| Left-censored Serfling | `survival::survreg` | `survreg(Surv(y, d, type = "left") ~ t + sin(2*pi*t/52) + cos(2*pi*t/52), dist = "lognormal")` | `d = 1`: an ordinary week; `d = 0`: an epidemic week. Iterated up to a predefined censoring share [@prochazka2016] |

: Implementing Serfling's method in R. {#tbl-serfl-r}

::: {.callout-warning title="A note on using fluserf"}
In the current source code, `y0_ul` is computed as `y0 + 1.645 × se.fit`, the standard
error of the fitted line rather than of the forecast. The threshold is therefore
narrower than the CDC's definition. Check it before using it in operation.
:::

A minimal example of the Serfling OLS model with percentile trimming and the two-week
rule:

```r
# df: weekly data with a column y (cases); the first 260 weeks are used for training
df$t  <- seq_len(nrow(df))
train <- df[df$t <= 260, ]
clean <- train[train$y <= quantile(train$y, 0.85), ]   # drop the highest 15% of weeks

m1 <- lm(y ~ t + cos(2*pi*t/52) + sin(2*pi*t/52), data = clean)
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + cos(4*pi*t/52) + sin(4*pi*t/52))
anova(m1, m2)                                           # is harmonic 2 needed?

new  <- df[df$t > 260, ]
pred <- predict(m1, newdata = new, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)
new$baseline  <- pred[, "fit"]
new$threshold <- pred[, "upr"]                          # baseline + 1.645 x forecast error
over          <- new$y > new$threshold
new$alarm     <- over & c(FALSE, head(over, -1))        # above the threshold 2 weeks running
```

## Comparison with other methods {#sec-serfl-compare}

Serfling works like a Shewhart control chart: each week is compared with the
threshold on its own. That catches sudden surges well but is less sensitive to slow,
smouldering rises [@unkel2012]. This section compares it with three commonly used
groups of methods.

### The Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) {#sec-serfl-mem}

MEM, developed by Vega and colleagues for influenza surveillance in Europe
[@vega2013], does not fit one wave to the whole year. It splits each past season into
pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic periods using the maximum accumulated rate
percentage (MAP) curve, and sets the threshold for a new season at the upper limit of
a one-sided confidence interval of the highest pre-epidemic values. On
influenza-like illness data from the French Sentinelles network, against an
expert-consensus gold standard, Souty and colleagues found [@souty2018]
(@fig-serfl-compare):

- Serfling (with percentile trimming) and MEM detected the epidemic start week
  equally well.
- Serfling had higher specificity and positive predictive value; MEM had higher
  sensitivity.
- Robust regression detected onsets less well and was the only method to split one
  epidemic season into two waves.

::: {#fig-serfl-compare}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-compare"></div>
```

Performance of four methods in detecting influenza epidemics on French data (figures
from Souty et al., 2018), each at its best detector. Choose a metric.
:::

### The Farrington algorithm {#sec-serfl-farrington}

The Farrington algorithm [@farrington1996] and Noufaily's improved version
[@noufaily2013] are widely used in European routine surveillance and available in R's
`surveillance` package [@salmon2016]. Farrington handles seasonality **through its
reference window**: for week $t_0$ it takes only the weeks within $\pm w$ of the same
time in the $b$ previous years (for example $w = 3$, $b = 5$) and fits a log-linear
quasi-Poisson model:

$$
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 t,\qquad Var\left(y_t\right) = \phi\,\mu_t
$$

Past epidemics are downweighted by their residuals, and the threshold is computed
after a 2/3 power transformation that makes even small counts close to normal:

$$
U_{t_0} = \hat{\mu}_{t_0}\left\{1 + \frac{2}{3}\, z_\alpha\,\frac{\left[\hat{\phi}\,\hat{\mu}_{t_0} + var\left(\hat{\mu}_{t_0}\right)\right]^{1/2}}{\hat{\mu}_{t_0}}\right\}^{3/2}
$$

With its quasi-Poisson structure and local window, Farrington suits low or sparse
counts better than classical Serfling. It does not account for serial
autocorrelation [@unkel2012].

### The cumulative sum control chart (CUSUM) {#sec-serfl-cusum}

CUSUM accumulates the positive standardised deviations over consecutive weeks:

$$
z_t = \frac{y_t - \mu_t}{\sigma_t},\qquad C_t = \max\left(0,\ C_{t-1} + z_t - k\right)
$$

and raises an alarm when $C_t > h$, where $k$ is the reference value and $h$ the
decision threshold [@unkel2012]. Accumulating over many weeks, CUSUM is more sensitive
than Serfling to small, sustained shifts. But it does not handle seasonality itself:
without a baseline model to standardise the data (Serfling's residuals, for example),
it raises false alarms every time the peak season begins.

### Summary table {#sec-serfl-table}

| Method | Modelling seasonality | Handling past epidemics | Alarm threshold | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serfling (OLS) | Fourier series over the whole year | Calendar exclusion, percentile trimming, iterative, robust or Tobit | $\hat{Y}_t + 1.645\,\hat{\sigma}_t$, crossed for ≥ 2 consecutive weeks | High specificity; separates trend from seasonality; easy to automate | Poor with small counts; needs regular seasonality |
| Serfling–Poisson (EuroMOMO) | Fourier series, fitted on spring and autumn weeks | Uses only weeks outside the epidemic season | Prediction interval, z-score | Suited to counts; population offset and delay correction | Assumes no excess mortality in spring and autumn |
| MEM | Splits the season into pre-, during and post-epidemic | Separates the epidemic period itself using the MAP curve | Upper limit of a one-sided confidence interval of pre-epidemic values | High sensitivity; distinguishes several intensity levels | Designed for single-peak epidemic seasons |
| Farrington | ±$w$ weeks around the same time in previous years | Downweights by residual | Threshold after a 2/3 power transformation | Suited to small counts; no assumed wave shape | Does not account for serial autocorrelation |
| CUSUM | Does not handle it alone; needs a baseline model | Resets the cumulative sum after an alarm | $C_t > h$ | Sensitive to small, sustained shifts | False alarms if the baseline model is wrong |

: Serfling compared with other methods. {#tbl-serfl-compare}

## Points to consider before applying it {#sec-serfl-apply}

Serfling assumes a clear seasonality that repeats steadily from year to year, with a
low period long enough to anchor the baseline [@unkel2012]. That usually holds for
influenza in temperate regions, with one winter peak a year, but not everywhere.
Before applying the method to a disease, indicator or area, check four points.

1. **A low period to anchor the baseline.** If a disease circulates all year,
   cutting out calendar weeks loses its basis, and what remains may still hold
   epidemic activity. Feng and colleagues, estimating influenza-associated mortality
   in China, used Serfling only for northern cities with a clear winter peak; in the
   subtropical south influenza circulated all year [@feng2012].
2. **The shape of the season.** Several peaks, asymmetric peaks or patterns that
   differ between regions may need more than one harmonic, so test $r$ on each area's
   own data. In northern Vietnam influenza can peak several times a year, in
   different seasons [@horby2012], and its seasonality in Vietnam is weak overall
   [@servadio2023].
3. **A stable peak timing.** The model gives every year the same wave with a fixed
   phase. If the peak moves a lot between years, an average baseline fits no year
   well, and last year's timing says little about next year's. In Vietnam the interval
   between influenza peaks varies much more than in temperate regions
   [@servadio2023].
4. **Performance in context.** Figures such as the high specificity in the French
   study come from one disease, indicator and surveillance system and may not carry
   over. Re-evaluate the method on the historical series of the disease and area to
   be monitored before using it in operation.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

- Serfling models the baseline as a long-term trend plus a Fourier series and sets
  the threshold about 1.645 standard deviations of the forecast error above it.
- Each harmonic is a cosine–sine pair, equivalent to one wave with an amplitude and a
  phase. The analyst chooses $r$ by testing; the data decide the coefficients.
- Cleaning the history is the decisive step: left in, past epidemics push the
  threshold too high. Each cleaning method fails in its own way, so test it on the
  series to be monitored.
- Requiring two consecutive weeks above the threshold reduces false alarms.
- The Poisson variant (such as EuroMOMO) suits counts; Farrington and CUSUM
  complement Serfling when counts are small or an epidemic rises slowly.
- In tropical regions, check the assumptions about seasonality first.
